subtype: Approach: overcorrecting with an extreme schedule [Pitfall]
passage: Imran taped a new chart above his desk in the Jaipur flat: 5 a.m. to 5 p.m., twelve hours of study, four backlogs and the fresh syllabus, all at once. "I'm going to make up the whole semester in a month," he told his flatmate Yogesh, who raised an eyebrow. "Twelve hours? You could not manage six last term." "Last term I was lazy." The first four days went well. On day nine he was reading the same paragraph three times. On day twelve he slept through the alarm, missed a class, and the chart stayed unticked all week. He pulled it off the wall, crumpled it, and dropped it in the bin. By Sunday he was not studying at all.

qa.q: How many hours of study did Imran's chart plan each day?
qa.a: The chart planned twelve hours of study.

qa.q: What is Imran feeling when he crumples the chart?
qa.a: Imran feels defeated and frustrated, tearing down the plan after failing to keep it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Imran use, and why?
qa.a: Imran could start with two hours a day and raise it slowly, because a plan that can be kept builds momentum where an extreme one collapses.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Imran's chart?
qa.a: Yogesh raises an eyebrow and points out that six hours was already too much last term, so Yogesh doubts the plan will hold.

grounding: Shows over-correcting after failure with an extreme timetable that collapses in the second week and is abandoned.

subtype: Approach: overcorrecting with an extreme schedule [Pitfall]
passage:
"Twelve hours a day, Dilnaz. From tomorrow. 6 am to 10 pm with breaks. I'm clearing all four backlogs in one go."
"All four? In one month?"
"I failed because I was lazy. So now I work double."
(Day 3)
"How's it going?"
"Great. Eleven and a half hours yesterday."
"You look grey, Amandeep."
"I'm fine."
(Day 9)
"You skipped the morning session."
"I couldn't get up. My head's pounding. I read the same page for an hour yesterday."
"Eat something first."
(Day 11)
"Are you studying today?"
"No. I've dropped the plan. I can't even keep a timetable."
"The plan was impossible. That's not the same as you being useless."
"Feels the same."
"Then let's make one you can actually keep. Four hours. Two subjects. Starting Monday."

qa.q: How many backlogs did Amandeep want to clear?
qa.a: All four backlogs in one go.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel on day 11?
qa.a: Amandeep felt defeated and discouraged, dropping the plan and feeling useless.

qa.q: What would you change first in Amandeep's plan?
qa.a: Start with a smaller, steady plan, like four hours on two subjects with sleep and meals built in, and add more only if it holds.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see Amandeep's collapse?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees the plan, not Amandeep, as the problem, and offers a realistic one to start again.

grounding: Shows a student planning twelve-hour study days to make up everything at once, collapsing in the second week and abandoning the plan.

subtype: Approach: overcorrecting with an extreme schedule [Pitfall]
passage: After failing three subjects in my second year, I decided to punish myself into success. I'm Kamal. I made a timetable with twelve hours of study every day: 5 am to 9 pm, twenty-minute meals, no phone. My roommate Zubin looked at it and said, "That's not a timetable, that's a sentence." I laughed and ignored him. The first week, I nearly managed it. By the middle of the second week I was sleeping through alarms, my eyes burned, and I couldn't remember a thing I'd read. On the tenth day I sat at my desk and felt nothing at all. I closed the book and didn't open another one for eight days. I'd gone from twelve hours to zero. Looking back, the failure wasn't that I was lazy. It was that I planned for a person who doesn't exist.

qa.q: What did Zubin call the timetable?
qa.a: That's not a timetable, that's a sentence.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel on the tenth day?
qa.a: Kamal felt empty and numb, sitting at the desk feeling nothing at all.

qa.q: What else could Kamal have tried after failing three subjects?
qa.a: Kamal could have started with a few steady hours a day and one subject at a time, adding more only after it held for a couple of weeks.

qa.q: How did Zubin see the timetable?
qa.a: Zubin saw it as a punishment rather than a plan, and tried to warn Kamal with a joke.

grounding: Illustrates a student overcorrecting with twelve-hour study days, burning out in the second week and dropping the plan entirely.
